title: Grade 3 Test Readiness
subtitle: Providence Home Academy · The Grade 3 standardized test · Two weeks at the end of Term 6

rows: The California Achievement Test (CAT), given by the parent at home
Georgia requires a national standardized test every three years, starting at the end of Grade 3 (then Grades 6, 9 and 12)
Readiness practice in **weeks 34–35**; the test in **week 36** or the week after
15–20 minutes, alongside the normal Term 6 work
Low. Georgia asks families to **keep** the results, not send them in

blocks.text: **Check before ordering.** Testing rules, versions and prices change. Confirm Georgia's current home-study requirements with the Georgia Department of Education, and the CAT's current versions and prices with the testing service.
We recommend one test for Grade 3: the **California Achievement Test**. Several homeschool testing services sell it, in paper and online versions.

items: **The parent can give it at home.** The child takes it at the kitchen table with a familiar adult, not in a strange room with a proctor.
**It's short and plain.** The sections are brief, and the questions are straightforward.
**It covers what Georgia asks for.** Reading, language arts and math. Some versions add science and social studies; either kind meets the requirement.
**It's affordable,** and the testing service scores it and sends back a report.

blocks.text: **Why not a stricter test for Grade 3?** It's the child's first standardized test. A calm first experience matters more than a precise national comparison. For later testing years, we may recommend a different test; that will come with those grades.

sections.title: The format is new, and that's fine

blocks.text: Providence Home Academy students learn by narration, recitation and short written checks. They tell back what they read, recite what they've memorized, and write their answers in their own words. A standardized test asks the same knowledge in a different shape:

head: What our students are used to
What the test does
rows: Telling back a story in their own words
Reading a short passage and choosing the best answer from four
Working until the job is done well
A parent who can see what they mean
A machine that reads only the bubble

blocks.text: A child who knows the material can still lose points to the format: rushing, skipping a line on the answer sheet, or freezing at a question they've never seen phrased that way. **The two weeks of readiness practice exist only to remove that obstacle.** A little practice with the test's shape is not a betrayal of how we teach; it's teaching the child one more kind of task.

sections.title: Low stakes: what to tell the child

blocks.text: "This is a check-up, like a visit to the doctor. It shows what you know. Nothing changes because of it. Do your best, and if a question is hard, choose your best guess and keep going."

items: **Don't grade or reward the score.** Record it and file it.
**No cramming.** Fifteen or twenty minutes a day is plenty.
**A normal week.** Regular bedtime, breakfast, and a walk outside before the test.

blocks.text: The report compares the child with a national group of children in the same grade. A **percentile** of 60 means the child scored as well as or better than 60 out of 100 children in that group. A **grade equivalent** of 4.2 means the child scored about as well as a typical child in the second month of Grade 4, not that they're ready for Grade 4 work.
**A low score in one area** usually points to a format problem or a topic not yet taught, not to a weak student. Check the gap review below before worrying.

week34.title: Test strategies
week34.text: **Test strategies** (below). Talk them through, then try them on the samples.

week35.title: A full practice round
week35.text: **A full practice round**: one sample set from each area with the answer sheet, under time. Then rest.

items: **Read every answer before choosing.** The first one that looks right may not be the best one.
**Cross out the answers you know are wrong** (on scrap paper, or in the test booklet if allowed). Choosing between two is easier than between four.
**Don't get stuck.** If a question is hard, make your best guess, mark it, and come back if there's time. There's usually no penalty for guessing.
**Keep your place.** Check that question 7 in the booklet goes in row 7 on the answer sheet. Every five questions, check again.
**For a reading passage,** read the questions first, so you know what to look for.
**In math,** estimate first. If the answer choices are 18, 81, 180 and 810, and you know it's "about 200," you're nearly there.

blocks.text: Fill in the bubble for the best answer. Practice on the answer sheet at the end.

passage.title: The Salt Box
passage.text: When Hannah's grandmother was a girl, there was no refrigerator in the farmhouse. In the fall, her father killed a hog and cut the meat into pieces. Hannah's grandmother helped rub each piece with salt and pack it into a wooden box. The salt drew the water out of the meat, and without water the meat could not spoil. All winter long, the family ate from the salt box. "Salt was worth more than sugar to us," Grandmother said.

questions.q: Why did the family put salt on the meat?
When did the family pack the meat?
In this story, the word **spoil** means:
What is this passage **mostly** about?
options: how one family kept meat through the winter

passage.title: The North Star
passage.text: Long ago, before there were maps on phones, travelers at night looked for one bright star. It sits almost exactly above the North Pole, so it stays in nearly the same place in the sky all night while the other stars seem to turn around it. Sailors called it the North Star. If you face it, you are facing north, and behind you is south. To find it, first find the Big Dipper. The two stars at the end of the Dipper's cup point straight to it.

questions.q: Why was the North Star useful to travelers?
options: It was the brightest light in the sky.
It showed which way was north.

questions.q: How do you find the North Star?
options: Follow the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's cup.

questions.q: If you face the North Star, what direction is behind you?

Which sentence is written correctly?

We went to boston in June.
we went to Boston in june.

**A missed question** is a clue, not a mark against the child. Was it the format (a bubble in the wrong row, a rushed choice), or a topic not yet taught? If it's a topic, look for it in the gap review.

A national Grade 3 test covers topics in an order that isn't ours. Most of what it asks, our students have learned in Grades 1–3; a few things come later in our sequence. Spend one short session on each "review" item.

head: Area
Covered in our curriculum
Review before the test
rows: Literature (Grade 3): reading and narrating whole books
**Main idea** ("what is this mostly about?") and **choosing among four answers**. Our students know the story; practice naming its main idea in one sentence.
**Synonyms and antonyms** by name ("same" and "opposite"); the prefixes **un-, re-, pre-**.
Grammar and Composition: parts of speech, sentence diagramming, capitalization and punctuation
**"Find the mistake"** questions; **I and me** ("Sarah and I went" / "with Sarah and me").
Picking the correct spelling **from a list** rather than writing it.
Arithmetic (Grade 3): facts, place value, money, time, measurement, perimeter and area, fractions, geometry, graphs
Little to review. **Rounding** to the nearest ten and hundred, and **reading a bar graph** quickly.
Life science (Grade 1) · Earth science and astronomy (Grade 2) · Chemistry and matter (Grade 3)
**Forces** (a push or a pull), **simple machines** (lever, ramp, pulley), and **light and sound**. These come in our Grade 4 physics year; a single short talk is enough.
History and Geography (Grade 3): maps, the fifty states, the three branches
**Map tools** (compass rose, map key, scale); **goods and services**, **needs and wants**; local government (the **mayor** leads a city, the **governor** a state).

items: **Order the test early,** at least a month ahead, so the materials arrive by week 34.
**Follow the test's own directions** exactly, including any time limits. A practice round is for practice; the real test is given by the rules.
**Keep the score report** with the Grade 3 portfolio and the year-end records. Georgia asks that it be kept, not sent.
**Don't change the curriculum** because of one score. If an area is low, check the gap review, and mention it at the start of Grade 4.
